substantiveFIRST.baseline: In original greater/smaller/equal order: zero, two, one intersections. All three reasons follow from perpendicular distance and circle radius.

Part1 intersects the circle centered at O of radius a with both rays. Part2 intersects the circle centered at interior M with each ray and retains all nonnegative ray parameters, not backward-line intersections. Each ray can have zero/one/two points. Selected nonconvex interior does not force forward perpendicular feet.
Two centers at distance r along the perpendicular through M, one on either side. Tangent-radius perpendicularity proves both construction and completeness for positive radius.
The unique tangent through the circle point is perpendicular to its radius there. Tangent-radius perpendicularity proves existence and uniqueness.

For noncollinear rays, use the open bisector ray of their smaller region, even if the selected source angle is nonconvex. Part1 infinitely many circles. Part2 at nonvertex P has exactly one; at vertex none. For a straight angle both rays can be tangent at the shared vertex: part1 infinitely many; part2 infinitely many at vertex, none at a nonvertex point.

Nonstraight locus is the smaller-region bisector ray without vertex, not both supporting-line bisectors and not a selected reflex bisector. Straight-angle locus is the complete perpendicular through the vertex minus the vertex.

Yes, unique common tangent through A perpendicular to the center line. Reflection of a hypothetical noncollinear A would create a second common point, proving center/A collinearity for both internal and external tangency.

Unique incircle from two internal angle bisectors. Equal perpendicular distances and forward-ray feet viewed from both ends of each side put contacts on the three finite segments. Excircles touching extensions do not solve the task.
Construct perpendicular foot H. If H differs from alleged nearest point O, a nondegenerate right-triangle argument gives AH<AO, contradiction. Therefore H=O and OA is perpendicular to p.
